algorithms.description: Model text as boxes, glue that can stretch and shrink, and penalties. Each potential breakpoint becomes a node, each feasible line an edge whose cost is a cubic function of how far the glue had to stretch or shrink, plus penalties for hyphenation and for consecutive lines whose looseness differs. Optimal breaking is then a shortest path through this directed acyclic graph, solved by dynamic programming with active-node pruning that keeps it near-linear in practice. The result is the visible difference between TeX and a browser: greedy first-fit optimises each line in isolation and cannot recover from an early mistake, while total-fit trades a slightly loose first line for three good ones after it. This is also the entry the catalogue's own README claimed was in the algorithm layer while it was not — and it belongs under graph algorithms rather than under typesetting, because the mechanism is a shortest path and the paper says so.
algorithms.citation: Knuth & Plass, Breaking paragraphs into lines, Software: Practice and Experience 11(11), 1119–1184

algorithms.name: Metaballs / blobby molecules
algorithms.summary: Sum a falling-off field around each point and take a level set. Nearby blobs merge into one smooth surface.
algorithms.eli5: Place a source in space whose influence falls off with distance. Sum several of them and take the surface where the total reaches a fixed value. Sources far apart give separate surfaces; bring them together and the surfaces bulge towards each other and merge, with no explicit operation required.
algorithms.description: Each source contributes a density that decays with distance — Blinn used a Gaussian, later work used cheaper polynomials with finite support — and the surface is an isosurface of the summed field. Because the field is a sum, blending is automatic and continuous: separate sources give separate components, and as they approach, the level set necks and merges without any explicit boolean. This is the earliest widely used implicit-surface modelling technique and the direct ancestor of SDF modelling, though the two differ in an important way that is easy to blur: a metaball field is a density, not a distance, so it does not support the sphere-tracing bound that makes raymarching efficient, and the polygonised result is what people historically used. Blinn's motivation was rendering electron density in molecular models, which is why the paper calls them blobby molecules. In generation they remain the right tool for organic masses defined by a handful of moving centres — clouds, slime, mercury, muscle bulk, cave chambers.
algorithms.citation: Blinn, A generalization of algebraic surface drawing, ACM Transactions on Graphics 1(3), 235–256

algorithms.name: Eller's algorithm
algorithms.summary: Generates a perfect maze one row at a time in constant memory. Infinite mazes with no backtracking.
algorithms.eli5: Build a maze one row at a time and never look back. Within the current row, randomly join some horizontally adjacent cells into groups, then ensure every group opens at least one passage down into the next row. Only one row is ever in memory, so the maze can be arbitrarily long.
algorithms.description: Process the maze row by row, holding only the current row. Each cell belongs to a set representing which cells are already connected. Within a row, randomly join horizontally adjacent cells whose sets differ, merging the sets. Then, for each set present in the row, carve at least one vertical passage down to the next row — at least one is what guarantees connectivity, and randomly carving more is what creates variety. Cells in the next row that received no vertical connection start fresh sets. On the final row, join every remaining distinct set horizontally to close the maze. The result is a perfect maze, generated in memory proportional to one row rather than the whole grid, which means the maze can be infinite in one direction — the only classic algorithm with that property. No paper; it circulated through hobbyist programming channels.
algorithms.citation: Marlin Eller, 1982; no original publication — described through hobbyist programming channels and documented in Buck, Mazes for Programmers, Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2015.

algorithms.name: Lloyd relaxation
algorithms.summary: Repeatedly move each site to the centroid of its Voronoi cell. Converges toward evenly sized, rounded cells.
algorithms.eli5: Scattered points produce uneven regions. So for each point, find the centre of its own region and move the point there. Recompute the regions and repeat. Each round makes them rounder and more equal in size, in the way soap bubbles settle against each other.
algorithms.description: Compute the Voronoi diagram of the current point set, move every point to the centroid of its own cell, then recompute and repeat. It converges toward a centroidal Voronoi tessellation, where each site sits exactly at its cell's centre of mass. Practically, it turns a clumpy random scatter into something that still reads as organic but has no slivers or giant cells — which is the difference between cobblestones that look laid and cobblestones that look spilled. Two or three iterations is usually enough; run it to convergence and the result drifts toward a hexagonal grid and stops looking natural. The same procedure is k-means clustering, arrived at from quantisation rather than geometry; Lloyd derived it at Bell Labs in 1957 but it went unpublished until 1982.
algorithms.citation: Least squares quantization in PCM, IEEE Trans. Information Theory 28(2), 129–137

algorithms.name: Morphological operators
algorithms.summary: Grow, shrink, open and close a region by sliding a shape over it. Set theory rather than arithmetic.
algorithms.eli5: Slide a chosen shape over a region. Keep the region wherever the shape fits entirely inside it, and everything thinner than the shape disappears. Do the reverse and the region grows, closing small holes. Shrink then grow, and specks vanish while everything larger survives at its original size — with edges staying hard throughout.
algorithms.description: Two primitives over a structuring element. Erosion keeps a pixel only where the element fits entirely within the region; dilation marks every pixel the element touches. Composing them gives opening — erode then dilate — which deletes anything smaller than the element while leaving larger regions at their original size, and closing, the reverse, which fills small gaps. Because the operations are defined by set containment rather than by averaging, edges stay hard: this is the correct tool where a blur-and-threshold would round corners and shift boundaries. Extended to greyscale by replacing containment with min and max, the same operators give local minimum and maximum filters, and the difference between dilation and erosion — the morphological gradient — is an edge detector with no smoothing. In generation this is the machinery of mask cleanup: removing single-cell speckle from a cellular-automata cave, closing one-tile gaps in a corridor, growing a wall by exactly two tiles, and separating touching blobs by repeated erosion.
algorithms.citation: Serra, Image Analysis and Mathematical Morphology, Academic Press, 1982; founded with Matheron at the École des Mines de Paris from 1964

algorithms.name: Median cut colour quantisation
algorithms.summary: Choose a palette by repeatedly splitting the colour cloud at its median along its longest axis.
algorithms.eli5: You need sixteen colours to represent a whole photograph. Put every pixel's colour in one box, find the direction the box extends furthest, and split it so that equal numbers of pixels fall on each side. Repeat on whichever box most needs it. Splitting by pixel count rather than by volume is what makes it spend the palette on the image's actual content.
algorithms.description: Put all pixel colours in one bounding box. Repeatedly select a box, find its longest dimension, and split it at the median along that dimension so that each half contains an equal *number of pixels* — not an equal volume, which is the key choice and the reason it beats uniform subdivision. Continue until the target palette size is reached, then take each box's mean as a palette entry. Splitting by population means colours that occupy a lot of the image get more palette entries, so a photograph of a face spends its palette on skin rather than on the one bright pixel in the corner. This is the algorithm behind GIF and PNG-8 palettes, and it is still the fastest reasonable answer for palette *extraction* — pulling a scheme out of a reference image — where k-means over CIELAB gives better results and Lloyd relaxation, already in this table, is how you would run it.
algorithms.citation: Heckbert, Color image quantization for frame buffer display, Computer Graphics (SIGGRAPH 82) 16(3), 297–307

algorithms.name: Midpoint displacement / diamond-square
algorithms.authors: Alain Fournier, Don Fussell, Loren Carpenter
algorithms.summary: Recursively subdivide and randomly offset midpoints to approximate fractional Brownian motion. Detail to any depth without storing it.
algorithms.eli5: Draw a straight line between two points, find its midpoint, and displace it by a random amount. You now have two shorter lines; do the same to each, but displace by half as much. Repeat, and a mountain profile emerges from a single straight line.
algorithms.description: Seed the four corners of a grid. The diamond step sets each square's centre to the average of its four corners plus a random offset; the square step sets each diamond's centre to the average of its four neighbours plus a random offset. Halve the offset range each round and recurse. How fast that range decays is the roughness parameter, and it corresponds to the Hurst exponent of the resulting surface — which is what ties the algorithm to real terrain, since measured landscapes have fractal roughness. The visible flaw is that the grid axes leak through as faint creases, because corner values are reused along rows and columns far more than diagonally.
algorithms.citation: Computer rendering of stochastic models, Communications of the ACM 25(6), 371–384

algorithms.name: Karplus–Strong string synthesis
algorithms.summary: A delay line of noise fed back through a one-pole averager. A plucked string from about four lines of code.
algorithms.eli5: Fill a short buffer with noise and play it repeatedly in a loop. On each pass, average each sample with the one beside it. The noise loses its harshness gradually, with the highest frequencies decaying first, which is exactly what a plucked string does.
algorithms.description: Fill a buffer of N samples with noise. Then repeatedly: output the oldest sample, and push back onto the buffer the average of that sample and the next one. The buffer length sets the pitch — the fundamental is the sample rate divided by N. The averaging is a low-pass filter applied once per period, so high harmonics lose energy far faster than low ones, which is exactly what a real string does as it decays. The initial noise burst supplies all harmonics at once, standing in for the pluck. It is startling how much instrument comes out of a delay line and an average, and it is the canonical demonstration that physical modelling beats sampling for variation.
algorithms.citation: Digital synthesis of plucked-string and drum timbres, Computer Music Journal 7(2), 43–55

algorithms.name: Liang hyphenation patterns
algorithms.summary: A packed trie of letter patterns with odd/even scores. Hyphenates correctly in a few kilobytes, no dictionary.
algorithms.eli5: How does software know that "hyphenation" breaks as hy-phen-a-tion? Not by knowing any words. A program was run over a dictionary to extract thousands of short letter patterns, each scored for and against breaking at that point. Add the scores at each gap; odd totals win.
algorithms.description: Rather than store a dictionary, Liang extracted patterns: short letter sequences, each carrying digits that vote for or against a break at each position. Odd values encourage a hyphen, even values forbid one, and higher values override lower. To hyphenate a word, match every pattern that occurs in it, take the maximum vote at each inter-letter position, and break where the result is odd. The pattern set is generated automatically from a hyphenated dictionary by a greedy procedure that repeatedly adds whichever patterns fix the most remaining errors, and it is stored in a packed trie of a few kilobytes. Note this is not a Markov model despite being learned from a corpus — the catalogue tags it `markov`, which is wrong; it is deterministic pattern matching with no probabilities at all.
algorithms.citation: Liang, Word Hy-phen-a-tion by Com-put-er, Stanford PhD thesis, 1983

algorithms.name: Mip pyramid / pyramidal parametrics
algorithms.summary: Precompute a chain of half-size copies of a field so any scale can be read in constant time.
algorithms.eli5: Keep the image, then a copy at half the width, then half of that, down to a single value. When something is far away, read from a small copy rather than averaging thousands of values from the large one. It costs a third more memory and converts an expensive question into one lookup.
algorithms.description: Build successive levels by averaging each 2×2 block, halving resolution each time, until a single sample remains. Because each level is a correctly band-limited version of the one above, sampling at the level matching the screen footprint gives a filtered result without touching more than a few samples, and blending between two levels — trilinear filtering — hides the transition. The total cost is 4/3 of the original, since 1 + 1/4 + 1/16 + … converges. For generation this is more than a rendering trick: the pyramid is a multi-scale decomposition of a field, so a mip chain over a heightfield gives cheap access to "average slope at kilometre scale", which is what biome rules, LOD selection and erosion pre-passes actually want. Williams introduced it as a solution to texture aliasing; its use as a general field summary came later.
algorithms.citation: Williams, Pyramidal parametrics, Computer Graphics (SIGGRAPH 83) 17(3), 1–11

algorithms.name: Simulated annealing
algorithms.authors: Scott Kirkpatrick, C. Daniel Gelatt, Mario Vecchi
algorithms.summary: Accept worsening moves with a probability that falls over time. Escapes local optima early, converges late.
algorithms.eli5: Hill-climbing stops at the first local peak. So permit occasional downhill moves — frequently at the start, rarely later, on a cooling schedule. Early on the search roams and finds the larger peaks; later it settles and climbs. Named after cooling metal slowly so its crystal structure forms properly.
algorithms.description: Borrowed directly from metallurgy: cool a metal slowly and its atoms settle into a low-energy crystal; quench it and they freeze into defects. The optimisation analogue proposes a random change to the current solution, always accepts it if it improves the objective, and accepts it anyway with probability exp(−Δ/T) if it worsens. The temperature T starts high, so early on the search wanders almost freely and cannot get trapped, then falls on a cooling schedule until only improvements are accepted. The cooling schedule is the whole art — too fast and it quenches into a poor local optimum, too slow and it costs more than exhaustive search. It needs no gradient, no population and barely any memory, which is why it is the default when you have a scoring function and an awkward discrete space, such as level layout or timetable repair.
algorithms.citation: Kirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi, Optimization by Simulated Annealing, Science 220(4598), 671–680

algorithms.name: D8 flow direction and accumulation
algorithms.summary: Send each cell's water to its steepest of eight neighbours, then count how many cells drain through each. Rivers appear as a threshold.
algorithms.eli5: Each cell sends its water to whichever of its eight neighbours is steepest downhill. Following those links lets you count, for every cell, how many cells upstream ultimately drain through it. Cells with a large count are channels, and the threshold you choose is effectively the drainage density.
algorithms.description: Assign each cell one of eight directions — the neighbour with the steepest downward drop, with diagonal distances scaled by √2. That single choice per cell turns the heightfield into a forest of trees rooted at the outlets, and accumulating cell counts up those trees gives contributing area: the number of cells whose water passes through each cell. Thresholding accumulation is the standard way to extract a channel network, and the threshold is effectively the drainage density dial. The method's limitation is built into the name: with only eight directions, flow on a planar hillside cannot spread and instead collapses into parallel lines one cell wide, which is what D-infinity and multiple-flow-direction schemes exist to fix. It is nonetheless the foundation everything else in the concept sits on, it requires depressions to have been filled first, and it is what lets a generated terrain place rivers, lakes, valleys and settlements from the heightfield alone.
algorithms.citation: O'Callaghan & Mark, The extraction of drainage networks from digital elevation data, Computer Vision, Graphics and Image Processing 28(3), 323–344

algorithms.name: Summed-area table
algorithms.summary: Store running sums so the total of any axis-aligned rectangle costs four lookups regardless of its size.
algorithms.eli5: Instead of storing each cell's value, store the total of everything above and to the left of it. The sum over any rectangle is then four of those totals added and subtracted: the large one, minus the two overhanging strips, plus the corner subtracted twice. Averaging over a thousand-cell region costs exactly what averaging over three cells costs.
algorithms.description: Each entry holds the sum of every sample above and to the left of it, computed in one pass. The sum over any axis-aligned rectangle is then S(x2,y2) − S(x1,y2) − S(x2,y1) + S(x1,y1): four reads, constant time, independent of the rectangle's size. That turns a box blur into an O(1)-per-pixel operation and, since a box blur applied three times approximates a Gaussian, makes large-radius blurs affordable. The catch is numerical: the running sums grow with area, so a large field in 32-bit floats loses precision at the far corner, which is why implementations use integers or tiles. Beyond blurring, it is the standard way to answer "how much of this is there, in this region" — local averages for adaptive thresholding, coverage for scattering rules, and the feature evaluation inside classic object detectors.
algorithms.citation: Crow, Summed-area tables for texture mapping, Computer Graphics (SIGGRAPH 84) 18(3), 207–212

algorithms.name: Perlin noise
algorithms.summary: Gradient noise on an integer lattice. Built in 1983 out of frustration with how machine-like Tron looked; Academy Award 1997.
algorithms.eli5: Assign a random direction to every corner of a grid. For a point in between, ask each surrounding corner how far along its own direction the point lies, and blend those answers. Neighbouring cells agree along the edge they share, so the result is smooth everywhere and the grid never shows.
algorithms.description: Every point of an integer lattice gets a pseudo-random unit gradient vector, derived by hashing its coordinates so no storage is needed and the result is the same everywhere, forever. To evaluate a sample, take the vector from each surrounding lattice corner to the sample point, dot it with that corner's gradient, and interpolate the results using a smooth ease curve. Because every gradient is dotted with a zero-length offset at its own corner, the function is exactly zero at every lattice point — which is the source of the faint axis-aligned grid that Perlin noise never entirely loses. Perlin's 2002 'Improving Noise' fixed two details: a fifth-order interpolant with zero second derivative at the ends, and a restricted gradient set that removes directional bias.
algorithms.citation: An Image Synthesizer, SIGGRAPH '85

algorithms.name: Value noise
algorithms.authors: No single origin; contemporaneous with Perlin noise
algorithms.summary: Hash a random value at each lattice point and interpolate between them. Cheaper and blobbier than gradient noise.
algorithms.eli5: Assign a random number to every corner of a grid and interpolate smoothly between them. Cheaper than the gradient version, but the random values sit exactly on the corners, so the grid shows through as a faint pattern of blobs.
algorithms.description: Assign a pseudo-random scalar to every lattice point by hashing its coordinates, then interpolate between the surrounding values with a smooth ease curve. That is the whole algorithm — it is what most people write first when asked to make smooth noise. The difference from Perlin noise is that Perlin stores gradients and takes dot products, so its value is zero at every lattice point and the extrema fall between them; value noise stores the values directly, so extrema land exactly on the lattice. The consequence is a more visible grid and a blobbier, lower-frequency character. It is cheaper, and for many uses — scattering weights, low-frequency variation, jitter — the difference is invisible and not worth the cost. No paper introduced it; it is the obvious construction, and it circulated as practice.
algorithms.citation: No origin publication. Documented in Ebert et al., Texturing & Modeling: A Procedural Approach.

algorithms.name: AC-4 arc consistency
algorithms.summary: Arc consistency with per-value support counters, so a deletion only wakes the values it actually affected. Optimal worst case.
algorithms.eli5: The same pruning, but instead of re-examining whole relationships when something changes, each value keeps a count of how many supporting values it still has and a record of which values it supports. Removing a value decrements exactly the counts that depended on it, and any count reaching zero removes another value in turn.
algorithms.description: AC-3 re-examines whole arcs when a domain changes, which repeats work. AC-4 instead precomputes, for every value, a counter of how many supporting values it has in each neighbouring variable and a list of the values it itself supports. Deleting a value decrements only the counters it supported; a counter reaching zero deletes that value in turn and cascades. This reaches the optimal worst-case bound O(e·d²) against AC-3's O(e·d³), at the cost of building the support structure up front — which is why AC-3 is often faster in practice on easy instances and AC-4 wins on hard ones. It earns a row here for one specific reason: Wave Function Collapse's reference implementation uses AC-4, not AC-3, and the per-value support counters are exactly the "compatible neighbour count" bookkeeping that WFC code is full of. Without this entry, the catalogue described WFC as constraint propagation while listing only the propagation algorithm WFC does not use.
algorithms.citation: Mohr & Henderson, Arc and path consistency revisited, Artificial Intelligence 28(2), 225–233

algorithms.name: FLIP
algorithms.summary: Hybrid particle-grid fluid: particles carry the state, a grid solves the pressure. Splashy without dissipating.
algorithms.eli5: Two representations of the same fluid, used together. Particles remember where the fluid is and which way it is moving, because particles never blur. A grid performs the calculation that stops the fluid compressing, because that needs neighbours in fixed positions. Each step transfers the information from one to the other and back.
algorithms.description: Pure grid methods lose detail because interpolating velocity each frame smears it — the fluid looks viscous when it should not. Pure particle methods struggle to enforce incompressibility. FLIP takes both: transfer particle velocities to a background grid, solve the pressure projection there to make the field divergence-free, then transfer the *change* in velocity back to the particles rather than the velocity itself. Because only the delta is interpolated, the particles retain their own high-frequency motion and nothing is smoothed away. That single choice is why FLIP looks energetic and splashy where its predecessor PIC looks like syrup, and blending between the two is the standard viscosity dial in production fluid solvers.
algorithms.citation: Brackbill & Ruppel, FLIP: A method for adaptively zoned, particle-in-cell calculations of fluid flows in two dimensions, J. Computational Physics 65(2), 314–343

algorithms.name: Fortune's sweepline
algorithms.summary: Sweeps a line across the plane maintaining a parabolic beach line, emitting Voronoi vertices as arcs vanish. O(n log n).
algorithms.eli5: Rather than computing every region at once, sweep a line across the plane and resolve each region only as the line reaches it. What trails behind the line is a curve made of parabolic arcs, and the corners of the finished diagram appear exactly where that curve intersects itself.
algorithms.description: Sweep a horizontal line down the plane. Behind it, maintain the 'beach line': a sequence of parabolic arcs, each the locus of points equidistant from one already-passed site and from the sweep line. Anything behind the beach line has its Voronoi cell finalised, because no future site can be closer. Two event types drive it — a site event, where the sweep line reaches a new point and inserts an arc, and a circle event, where an arc is squeezed to nothing between its neighbours and a Voronoi vertex is emitted at the circumcentre. Both structures are balanced trees, giving O(n log n) time and O(n) space, which is optimal. The cleverness is the beach line: it converts a global nearest-neighbour problem into a local one.
algorithms.citation: A sweepline algorithm for Voronoi diagrams, Proc. 2nd Annual Symposium on Computational Geometry, 313–322 (also Algorithmica 2, 1987)

algorithms.name: Damped least-squares Jacobian IK
algorithms.authors: Charles Wampler; independently Yoshihiko Nakamura and Hideo Hanafusa
algorithms.summary: Linearise the whole chain into a matrix, solve for joint changes, and damp the solve so singular poses do not explode.
algorithms.eli5: Work out, for each joint, which way the hand would move if that joint rotated slightly. That gives a matrix relating all the joints to the hand. Invert it to find the joint changes that move the hand where you want. The difficulty: when the limb is fully extended the matrix becomes unsolvable and the answer diverges — so a damping term is added, trading a little accuracy for never diverging.
algorithms.description: The Jacobian relates joint velocities to end-effector velocity. Inverting it — or pseudo-inverting it, since chains are usually redundant — gives the joint change needed for a desired end-effector change, applied iteratively. Near a singularity, where the chain loses a degree of freedom because it is fully extended or aligned, the pseudo-inverse's singular values approach zero and the requested joint velocities approach infinity, producing the violent snapping that plagued early IK. Damped least squares solves min ‖JΔθ − Δx‖² + λ²‖Δθ‖² instead, which bounds the solution at the cost of not reaching the target exactly; λ is the whole trade, and adaptive schemes raise it only near singularities. Unlike CCD and FABRIK, this formulation generalises cleanly to multiple simultaneous targets, orientation as well as position, joint-limit and balance constraints via null-space projection, and weighted priorities — which is why full-body and robotics solvers are built on it while games often prefer the cheaper heuristics.
algorithms.citation: Wampler, Manipulator inverse kinematic solutions based on vector formulations and damped least-squares methods, IEEE Trans. Systems, Man and Cybernetics 16(1), 93–101 (1986); Nakamura & Hanafusa, Inverse kinematic solutions with singularity robustness, ASME J. Dynamic Systems 108, 1986

algorithms.name: Boids
algorithms.summary: Three steering rules per agent — separation, alignment, cohesion — and flocking emerges with no leader.
algorithms.eli5: Give each bird three rules: avoid collisions with neighbours, match their heading, and move towards the centre of those nearby. No individual leads and none plans. A flock forms regardless.
algorithms.description: Each agent looks only at neighbours within a local radius and applies three steering urges: separation, to avoid crowding; alignment, to match their average heading; cohesion, to move toward their average position. Sum them, weight them, clamp to a maximum force, and integrate. Nothing computes the flock — there is no leader, no global plan, and no agent knows the flock exists — yet the aggregate motion is convincingly organic, splits around obstacles and rejoins. Reynolds' framing mattered as much as the rules: he presented it as an alternative to scripting each bird's path, which is the general argument for emergent generation over authored content. The tuning trap is that the three weights interact non-linearly; too much cohesion collapses the flock to a point, too much separation disperses it entirely, and the pleasing band between them is narrow.
algorithms.citation: Reynolds, Flocks, Herds, and Schools: A Distributed Behavioral Model, SIGGRAPH '87, Computer Graphics 21(4), 25–34

algorithms.name: BSP-tree set operations
algorithms.summary: Union, difference and intersection evaluated by merging BSP trees. Exact boolean modelling on arbitrary polyhedra.
algorithms.eli5: To cut one solid out of another you must know which parts of each surface lie inside the other. So divide both solids into pieces, using each other's faces as cutting planes, until every piece is unambiguously inside or outside. Then discard the pieces you do not want and rejoin the rest.
algorithms.description: Represent each solid as a BSP tree whose leaves are labelled inside or outside — this is an exact representation of an arbitrary polyhedron, not an approximation. A boolean is then computed by merging one tree into the other: push the second solid's tree down through the first's planes, splitting it as it goes, and combine the in/out labels at the leaves according to the operation. Because everything is decided by which side of a plane a region lies on, the result is topologically exact and closed by construction. This is the classical answer to why CSG is easier than mesh booleans: mesh-based approaches have to compute intersection curves between surfaces and stitch them, which is numerically fragile, whereas BSP reduces the whole problem to plane classification.
algorithms.citation: Thibault & Naylor, Set operations on polyhedra using binary space partitioning trees, SIGGRAPH '87, Computer Graphics 21(4), 153–162

algorithms.name: Katz back-off
algorithms.summary: When an n-gram was never seen, fall back to the shorter context rather than assigning zero probability.
algorithms.eli5: The three-letter sequence you need never occurred in the corpus, so its probability is zero and generation stops. The remedy: take a little probability away from every sequence that was observed, and give the pooled remainder to the shorter two-letter estimate. Ask for three, fall back to two, fall back to one.
algorithms.description: Raw n-gram counts assign probability zero to anything unobserved, which is fatal — a single unseen bigram makes an entire generated sequence impossible. Katz back-off discounts the observed counts slightly, freeing a mass of probability, then redistributes it by falling back to the (n−1)-gram model whenever the full context has too few observations to trust. The fallback recurses down to unigrams. The practical effect for a name generator or a text model is that it can produce combinations absent from the corpus while still preferring ones the corpus supports — which is exactly the balance between plagiarism and gibberish that determines whether generated names feel authentic.
algorithms.citation: Estimation of probabilities from sparse data for the language model component of a speech recogniser, IEEE Trans. ASSP 35(3), 400–401

algorithms.name: Loop subdivision
algorithms.summary: Split every triangle into four and average positions. The triangle counterpart to Catmull–Clark.
algorithms.eli5: Divide every triangle into four by marking the midpoint of each edge, then move every vertex, old and new, towards a weighted average of its neighbours. Repeat, and a faceted triangle mesh becomes smooth while remaining made of triangles — which matters, because renderers and physics engines want triangles.
algorithms.description: Each edge gets a new vertex at a weighted average of its two endpoints and the two opposite vertices of its adjacent triangles; each original vertex moves towards the average of its neighbours by an amount depending on its valence. Splitting each triangle into four keeps the mesh triangular throughout, which is the whole reason to prefer it: renderers, physics engines and GPU pipelines want triangles, so a triangle-in, triangle-out scheme avoids a conversion. The limit surface is a quartic box spline, C² except at irregular vertices where it is C¹ — the same caveat as Catmull–Clark, and the valence-dependent weight is precisely the tuning that makes those points as smooth as they can be. Loop introduced it in a master's thesis rather than a paper, which is why it is often cited indirectly. In generation it is the natural smoother for anything that came out of marching cubes or a triangle-based sculpt, and it is what libigl and most geometry-processing libraries provide.
algorithms.citation: Loop, Smooth Subdivision Surfaces Based on Triangles, master's thesis, Department of Mathematics, University of Utah, 1987

algorithms.name: Marching cubes
algorithms.summary: Turns a sampled scalar field into a triangle mesh by table lookup, one cube at a time. The most cited paper in computer graphics.
algorithms.eli5: You have a grid of values and want the surface where they cross zero. Examine each cube of eight neighbouring values and record which corners are inside and which are outside. There are only 256 possibilities, so look up the corresponding piece of surface in a table and join all the pieces together.
algorithms.description: Sample the field on a regular grid. For each cube of eight neighbouring samples, each corner is either inside or outside the isosurface, giving 256 possible sign configurations — reduced to 15 distinct cases by rotation and reflection symmetry, and baked into a lookup table of triangle topologies. For each edge that crosses the surface, linearly interpolate along it to find where the field hits the threshold, and emit the triangles the table specifies. It is fast, embarrassingly parallel, and needs no global information, which is why it is everywhere. Two known weaknesses: sharp creases get rounded off, because vertices only ever land on cube edges; and several configurations are genuinely ambiguous, producing holes unless a disambiguation scheme is added.
algorithms.citation: Marching cubes: A high resolution 3D surface construction algorithm, SIGGRAPH '87, Computer Graphics 21(4), 163–169

algorithms.name: Marching squares
algorithms.authors: No origin publication; the 2D specialisation of marching cubes
algorithms.summary: Trace the contour line where a field crosses a threshold, one grid cell at a time, from a 16-case table.
algorithms.eli5: You have a grid of values and want the line where they cross a threshold. Examine each square of four values and record which corners are above and which below. There are sixteen possibilities, so look up how the line cuts through and join all the segments. Two of the sixteen are genuinely ambiguous and have to be resolved by testing the centre.
algorithms.description: For each cell of four samples, the four above-or-below bits index a table of 16 configurations giving the line segments crossing that cell. Linear interpolation along the cut edges places each endpoint at the actual crossing rather than at the cell boundary, which is the difference between a smooth isoline and a staircase. Two of the sixteen cases are saddles where the four corners alternate, and the table has to pick a joining — a genuine ambiguity, usually resolved by testing the cell centre. This is the machinery behind contour maps, shaded relief, coastline extraction from a heightfield, and the outline of any 2D metaball or SDF blob. It has no origin paper because it is the two-dimensional restriction of marching cubes, and was in use before anyone thought it needed naming separately.
algorithms.citation: No origin paper. The 2D case of Lorensen & Cline's marching cubes (1987); the ambiguous saddle cases and their resolution are discussed throughout the isosurface literature.

algorithms.name: Answer set programming
algorithms.summary: Declare rules and constraints in logic; the solver returns stable models — every valid world, not just one.
algorithms.eli5: Describe the world as rules of the form "this holds if those hold, unless that is known". Then ask not for a yes-or-no answer but for every complete, self-consistent world in which all the rules are true. Each of those worlds is one valid generated result.
algorithms.description: Write a logic program of rules and integrity constraints. Its stable models — the answer sets — are exactly the consistent worlds satisfying it, and a solver enumerates them. The distinctive feature for content generation is that it produces *all* valid solutions rather than one, which makes it possible to sample uniformly from the space of legal artefacts instead of taking whatever a search happens to reach first. It also supports default reasoning: rules can hold unless contradicted, which maps naturally onto design constraints of the form 'rooms connect to corridors unless they are secret'. Answer set programming has a real if small following in PCG research — Smith and Mateas argued for it as a general framing where the designer writes what must be true and the solver handles the rest.
algorithms.citation: Gelfond & Lifschitz, The stable model semantics for logic programming, ICLP/SLP 1988, 1070–1080

algorithms.name: Granular synthesis
algorithms.authors: Curtis Roads, building on Dennis Gabor and Iannis Xenakis
algorithms.summary: Build sound from thousands of millisecond-long fragments. Control the cloud statistically rather than the waveform directly.
algorithms.eli5: Cut a sound into fragments a few thousandths of a second long, then play thousands of fragments per second, choosing which ones and at what pitch and volume within limits you set. Individually they are clicks; collectively they are a texture, and controlling the statistics rather than the waveform is what lets you stretch, freeze or blur the source.
algorithms.description: Each grain is a short windowed segment — typically 1 to 100 ms — with its own source position, amplitude, pitch and pan, and the output is the sum of many overlapping grains. Control is statistical: grain density, the distribution of pitches, how far source positions scatter, and the window shape, which matters because an abrupt window makes every grain audible as a click. The regime changes qualitatively with density and grain length, from discrete pointillistic events through a rough texture to a continuous tone, and that boundary is the expressive territory. Gabor's 1946 acoustic quantum is the theoretical origin and Xenakis composed with the idea in the 1950s, but Roads is where it becomes a synthesis technique with parameters. For generation it is the cheapest way to get endless non-repeating variation from one recorded source — wind, crowds, rain, fire, machinery — and it is also how time-stretching without pitch change works, since grains can be replayed at a different rate than they were extracted.
algorithms.citation: Roads, Introduction to granular synthesis, Computer Music Journal 12(2), 11–13 (1988); theoretical origin in Gabor, Theory of communication, J. IEE 93, 1946

algorithms.name: Iterated function systems
algorithms.summary: A handful of contractive affine maps applied at random. Their attractor is a fractal — the Barnsley fern from four transforms.
algorithms.eli5: Write down three or four transformations that each shrink and tilt the plane. Start from a point, apply one at random, mark where you land, and repeat a million times. The marks accumulate into a fern — and that fern is the only image those transformations could ever have produced.
algorithms.description: Take a small set of affine transformations, each of which contracts distances. Whatever shape you start from, applying the set repeatedly converges to a single attractor determined entirely by the transforms — Hutchinson's theorem — so the fractal is fully specified by a few rows of numbers. The chaos game evaluates it cheaply: start at any point, repeatedly pick one transform at random with assigned probabilities, apply it, and plot the result. After discarding the first few iterations the points land on the attractor and nowhere else. Barnsley's fern needs four transforms, one of which is applied only one per cent of the time to make the stem. The compression implication was the original excitement: an image reduced to twenty-four numbers.
algorithms.citation: Barnsley, Fractals Everywhere, Academic Press, 1988; Hutchinson, Fractals and self similarity, Indiana Univ. Math. J. 30, 1981

algorithms.name: Musgrave hydraulic and thermal erosion
algorithms.authors: F. Kenton Musgrave, Craig Kolb, Robert Mace
algorithms.summary: The first erosion pass applied to fractal terrain. Water carries sediment downhill; talus slides until it is below the angle of repose.
algorithms.eli5: Two passes over a heightfield. The first drops rain on every cell and lets it dissolve material, run downhill, and deposit that material where it slows. The second checks whether any slope exceeds what loose material can hold and, if so, moves material down until it does not. Rivers come from the first, scree slopes from the second.
algorithms.description: Two separate processes run over a heightfield. Thermal erosion handles material loosened and falling: for each cell, compare height with its neighbours, and wherever the slope exceeds a fixed talus angle, move a fraction of the difference downhill. Repeated, this produces the constant-angle scree slopes real cliffs accumulate at their base. Hydraulic erosion adds water: each cell holds some water and dissolved sediment, water flows to lower neighbours carrying sediment with it, sediment beyond the water's capacity is deposited, and some water evaporates each step. The result is drainage — connected channels, deposition in valleys — which is exactly the structure that pure fractal noise cannot have, and why this paper marks the point terrain stopped looking like crumpled paper.
algorithms.citation: The synthesis and rendering of eroded fractal terrains, SIGGRAPH '89, Computer Graphics 23(3), 41–50

algorithms.name: SIMP density-based topology optimisation
algorithms.authors: Martin Bendsøe; power-law penalisation with Ole Sigmund
algorithms.summary: Give every cell a density between empty and solid, penalise the in-between, and follow the gradient. The whole method is 99 lines.
algorithms.eli5: Rather than choosing a shape, give every element of the block a density between empty and solid. Run the physics, and calculate for each element how much stiffer the structure would be if it held more material. Move material from the elements contributing least to those contributing most, keeping the total constant, and repeat. Penalising intermediate densities is what forces the answer towards solid or empty rather than a uniform grey.
algorithms.description: Discretise the design domain into finite elements and let each carry a density variable. Stiffness is scaled as density to a power — typically three — which is the "penalisation": intermediate densities become inefficient, so the optimiser is pushed towards a nearly black-and-white answer without an explicit integer constraint. Each iteration solves the finite-element problem, computes the sensitivity of compliance to each density analytically, and updates all densities at once by an optimality-criteria rule subject to a volume constraint. Two fixes are not optional and are why naive implementations fail: a sensitivity or density filter over a fixed radius, which removes the checkerboard instability and makes the answer independent of mesh resolution, and a move limit for stability. This is what commercial "generative design" runs, and Sigmund's 99-line MATLAB implementation — 36 lines of main program, 12 of optimiser, 16 of filter, 35 of finite elements — is the reference specification, later reduced to 88 by vectorising.
algorithms.citation: Bendsøe, Optimal shape design as a material distribution problem, Structural Optimization 1, 193–202 (1989); the reference implementation is Sigmund, A 99 line topology optimization code written in Matlab, Structural and Multidisciplinary Optimization 21, 120–127 (2001)

algorithms.name: Cyclic coordinate descent (CCD)
algorithms.summary: Rotate one joint at a time to aim the end effector at the target, walking back from the tip. One equation, one unknown.
algorithms.eli5: Work backwards from the hand. Rotate the wrist so the hand points as close to the target as it can, then the elbow, then the shoulder, then repeat the sweep. It always converges and requires no mathematics harder than an angle, and it tends to over-rotate whichever joint is nearest the target.
algorithms.description: Start at the joint nearest the end effector. Rotate that joint by the single angle that best aligns the vector from joint to end effector with the vector from joint to target — a one-line calculation from the angle between two vectors. Move to the next joint down the chain and repeat, then loop back to the tip and go again. Each step reduces the error monotonically, and each involves one degree of freedom, so there is nothing to invert and nothing to tune. It converges quickly for short chains and is trivial to implement, which is why it is everywhere in games. Its characteristic artefact is that joints near the end effector absorb most of the rotation, giving a curled, over-bent wrist unless you weight or limit the per-joint rotation.
algorithms.citation: A combined optimization method for solving the inverse kinematics problem of mechanical manipulators, IEEE Trans. Robotics and Automation 7(4), 489–499

algorithms.name: Eigenfaces (PCA shape models)
algorithms.summary: Principal component analysis over aligned faces. The eigenvectors become the sliders.
algorithms.eli5: Average a thousand photographed faces, then ask along which directions real faces differ most from that average. The answer is a few dozen difference images. Any face is then the average plus a measured amount of each — so a face has become a list of a few dozen numbers.
algorithms.description: Treat each aligned face image as a point in a very high-dimensional space — one dimension per pixel — and run principal component analysis over a population of them. The leading eigenvectors are directions of greatest variation, and they turn out to be interpretable: overall lightness, then broad shape, then progressively finer structure. Any face is then approximated by the mean plus a weighted sum of a few dozen components, so a whole face is described by a few dozen numbers. This is the ancestor of every morphable model that followed, and it establishes the pattern the whole `morph` concept rests on: don't write rules for what a face can be, measure a population and let the principal components be the parameters. Its limits are equally instructive — everything must be aligned first, and pushing the weights beyond the range seen in the data produces monsters.
algorithms.citation: Turk & Pentland, Eigenfaces for Recognition, J. Cognitive Neuroscience 3(1), 71–86

algorithms.name: Marching tetrahedra
algorithms.summary: Split each cube into tetrahedra before contouring, removing marching cubes' ambiguous cases.
algorithms.eli5: The cube version has configurations where the corner values genuinely do not determine how the surface connects, and choosing wrongly leaves holes. Subdividing each cube into tetrahedra first removes the problem: four corners admit almost no cases and none of them is ambiguous. The cost is more triangles, of worse shape.
algorithms.description: Marching cubes has configurations where the sign pattern at the eight corners does not determine the surface topology, and choosing wrongly leaves holes between adjacent cells. Marching tetrahedra sidesteps this by decomposing each cube into five or six tetrahedra first. A tetrahedron has only four corners and therefore just two distinct cases up to symmetry — one corner separated, or two-and-two — and neither is ambiguous, so the resulting mesh is always watertight. The cost is roughly three times as many triangles for the same field, and a visible bias in triangle orientation from the fixed decomposition. It is the usual choice when correctness matters more than triangle count, and the reason it appears in GPU and differentiable pipelines is that the case table is small enough to branch on cheaply.
algorithms.citation: Doi & Koide, An efficient method of triangulating equi-valued surfaces by using tetrahedral cells, IEICE Trans. Information and Systems E74-D(1), 214–224

algorithms.name: Mitchell's best-candidate
algorithms.summary: Generate k random candidates, keep the one furthest from existing samples. Approximate blue noise in five lines.
algorithms.eli5: To place a point well, do not simply choose one position. Generate ten candidate positions and keep whichever is furthest from every point already placed, discarding the rest. Almost trivially simple, and the result looks deliberately scattered.
algorithms.description: To add a point, generate k random candidates and keep whichever is furthest from any already-placed sample. Increasing k improves the blue-noise quality and the cost; k around ten is the usual compromise. It is strictly worse than Bridson's method on both spectral quality and asymptotic cost, but it fits in a few lines, needs no background grid, works over any domain you can sample and measure distance in — including surfaces and non-uniform densities — and never fails to place a point. That last property matters: Poisson disk sampling with a fixed radius can simply run out of room, whereas best-candidate degrades gracefully. It is the right choice when you want approximately even scatter without infrastructure.
algorithms.citation: Mitchell, Spectrally optimal sampling for distribution ray tracing, SIGGRAPH '91, Computer Graphics 25(4), 157–164

algorithms.name: Digital waveguide synthesis
algorithms.summary: Model a string or tube as two delay lines carrying waves in opposite directions. Physical modelling for the cost of a buffer.
algorithms.eli5: A wave on a string travels in both directions and reflects at each end, so model it as two delay lines running in opposite directions with a filter at each termination. Sum them to hear the string. It costs almost nothing to compute and behaves like a real string because it is the same equations, solved exactly.
algorithms.description: The one-dimensional wave equation has an exact solution as the sum of two travelling waves moving in opposite directions, so a string or air column can be simulated as a pair of delay lines with reflection filters at the terminations — the filters encode how much energy is lost and which frequencies are damped at each end. Excitation is an impulse or a noise burst injected into the lines; the output is the sum at a pickup position. Because the underlying solution is exact, the model is not an approximation of a string but a discretisation of one, which is why it responds correctly to physical changes: shorten the delay and the pitch rises, stiffen the reflection filter and the tone brightens, add a nonlinearity at one end and you get a bowed or reed instrument rather than a plucked one. Karplus–Strong, already in this table, is the minimal special case — one delay line and a two-point averaging filter — and the waveguide formulation is the theory that explains why it works and how to extend it.
algorithms.citation: Smith, Physical modeling using digital waveguides, Computer Music Journal 16(4), 74–91

algorithms.name: Genetic programming
algorithms.summary: Evolve programs rather than parameter strings. Individuals are expression trees, and crossover swaps subtrees.
algorithms.eli5: The same selection loop, except what is being evolved is small programs shaped as trees rather than lists of numbers. Combining two survivors means exchanging a subtree, so the offspring is a working program that nobody wrote and nobody has read.
algorithms.description: Instead of a fixed-length chromosome, each individual is a program — usually an expression tree over a chosen function and terminal set. Crossover swaps randomly chosen subtrees between two parents, and mutation replaces a subtree with a fresh random one. Because the representation is variable-size, the search explores structures rather than just parameter values, which is what lets it discover the *form* of a solution and not merely tune one. In generation this is how you evolve shaders, textures, plant grammars, and behaviour trees — the classic result being that evolved expressions produce imagery nobody would have written by hand. Its characteristic pathology is bloat: trees grow ever larger with introns that do nothing, because neutral code is protective against destructive crossover, so implementations need explicit size pressure.
algorithms.citation: Koza, Genetic Programming: On the Programming of Computers by Means of Natural Selection, MIT Press, 1992

algorithms.name: Void-and-cluster blue noise
algorithms.summary: Build a blue-noise mask by repeatedly finding the biggest gap and the tightest cluster, and swapping between them.
algorithms.eli5: Start from a random binary pattern. Blur it to find the densest cluster and the emptiest void, then move a point from the cluster into the void. Repeat until nothing improves. Then remove and re-add the points in order, recording the order as a rank — which yields a tile whose every threshold level is itself well distributed.
algorithms.description: Start from a random binary pattern. Filter it with a Gaussian to measure local density, then locate the tightest cluster — the 1 in the densest neighbourhood — and the largest void — the 0 in the sparsest — and move that 1 into that 0. Iterate to convergence, which yields a maximally uniform binary pattern. The clever second half is the ranking phase: remove points one at a time, always the tightest cluster, recording the order, then add points back into the largest voids, again recording the order. The resulting rank per pixel, normalised, is a threshold mask whose every threshold level is itself a good blue-noise pattern — which is what makes it usable as a dither array, and later as the precomputed blue-noise texture that real-time renderers use for sample offsets, stochastic transparency and temporal accumulation. Unlike Poisson-disk sampling it produces a tileable array of *values* rather than a set of positions, which is the form a shader can consume for free.
algorithms.citation: Ulichney, The void-and-cluster method for dither array generation, Proc. SPIE 1913, Human Vision, Visual Processing and Digital Display IV, 332–343

algorithms.name: Material point method
algorithms.authors: Deborah Sulsky, Zhen Chen, Howard Schreyer; brought into graphics by Stomakhin, Schroeder, Chai, Teran & Selle
algorithms.summary: Particles carry material state, a grid computes forces. Handles snow, sand, mud and goo in one solver.
algorithms.eli5: Particles carry what the material is: how compressed, how sheared, how much it has failed. A background grid computes the forces, because forces need to know what is adjacent to what. Particles hand their state to the grid, the grid resolves the forces, and the particles collect the result and move. One solver covers snow, sand, mud and jelly.
algorithms.description: A continuum method on a hybrid representation: particles hold mass, velocity and — crucially — a deformation gradient recording how the material around them has been stretched and sheared since rest. Each step transfers state to a background grid, computes forces there from a constitutive model applied to the deformation gradient, updates velocities, and transfers back. Changing the constitutive model changes the material without changing the solver, which is why one implementation covers snow, sand, mud, foam and viscoelastic goo. Stomakhin's paper added elastoplasticity with hardening — snow compacts as it deforms and stops springing back — and was written for Disney's *Frozen*, which is a good illustration of production driving the research rather than the reverse. Its lineage matters and is easy to miss: MPM was built as an extension of FLIP — already in this table — from fluids to solid mechanics, the addition being that each particle carries the full stress tensor so that history-dependent constitutive models become possible. The 2013 snow paper is what made it famous in graphics, and is where the sand, mud and goo variants come from, but the method is nineteen years older than that.
algorithms.citation: Sulsky, Chen & Schreyer, A particle method for history-dependent materials, Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 118, 179–196 (1994). Graphics introduction: Stomakhin et al., A material point method for snow simulation, ACM TOG 32(4) (SIGGRAPH 2013)

algorithms.name: Ridged multifractal
algorithms.summary: Invert the absolute value of each noise octave and weight it by the previous one. Sharp ridges, not rounded hills.
algorithms.eli5: Take a layer of noise and fold it: wherever it dips below zero, flip it back up. Smooth valleys become sharp creases. Stack several folded layers, letting each appear only where the layer above was already high, and you get ridgelines with side spurs rather than rounded hills.
algorithms.description: Take the absolute value of a signed noise octave and subtract it from one. The absolute value creates a crease wherever the noise crosses zero, and inverting turns that crease into a ridge rather than a valley. Summed across octaves this gives sharp crests — mountain ridgelines, mineral veins, lightning-like filaments — where plain fBm gives rounded lumps. Musgrave's addition beyond the basic trick is the multifractal part: weight each octave by the value of the previous one, so detail only appears where the coarser scale was already high. That is what makes the ridges sharp on peaks and the valleys smooth, which is how real terrain behaves and what plain fBm gets wrong by applying the same roughness everywhere. Published in the Texturing & Modeling book rather than as a paper.
algorithms.citation: Musgrave, in Ebert, Musgrave, Peachey, Perlin & Worley, Texturing & Modeling: A Procedural Approach, Academic Press, first edition 1994 — a book chapter, not a paper.

algorithms.name: Delaunay refinement
algorithms.authors: Jim Ruppert, building on L. Paul Chew (1989)
algorithms.summary: Insert circumcentres of bad triangles until every angle clears a bound. Meshes with a mathematical quality guarantee.
algorithms.eli5: You have a triangulation, but some triangles are thin slivers, which make numerical simulation unreliable. Take the worst one, insert a new point at the centre of its circumcircle, and re-triangulate. No sliver survives that. Repeat until none is too thin — and it is provable that this terminates.
algorithms.description: A Delaunay triangulation of scattered points contains slivers — thin triangles that wreck numerical simulation. Refinement fixes this by adding points: find any triangle whose smallest angle falls below a threshold, insert its circumcentre as a new vertex, and re-triangulate. Each insertion destroys the offending triangle, and the surprising result is that the process terminates rather than cascading forever, with the mesh size within a constant factor of optimal. Chew's 1989 technical report established the first such guarantee at 30°; Ruppert extended it to graded meshes with varying element size and boundary constraints. This is why FEM and CFD meshes can be generated automatically at all, and it is the same insertion idea used to grade Voronoi cell sizes for procedural districts.
algorithms.citation: Ruppert, A Delaunay refinement algorithm for quality 2-dimensional mesh generation, J. Algorithms 18(3), 548–585; Chew, Guaranteed-quality triangular meshes, Cornell TR 89-983

algorithms.name: Kneser–Ney smoothing
algorithms.summary: Back off on how many distinct contexts a word appears in, not how often it appears. The best-performing n-gram smoothing.
algorithms.eli5: "Francisco" is a common word, but almost only after "San". So when estimating what follows an unfamiliar context, do not ask how often a word occurs — ask in how many distinct contexts it has occurred. Words that appear only inside one fixed phrase are demoted, which is why this outperforms every other counting method.
algorithms.description: Ordinary back-off falls back to raw unigram frequency, which misfires on words that are common but contextually narrow. The stock example is 'Francisco': it appears often, but almost only after 'San', so backing off to its frequency makes it a plausible continuation everywhere, which it is not. Kneser–Ney instead builds the lower-order distribution from *continuation counts* — how many distinct contexts a word has followed — so 'Francisco' scores low despite being frequent. Combined with absolute discounting, subtracting a fixed amount from every observed count, it reliably gives the lowest perplexity of any n-gram method. For generation it is the difference between a name generator that produces convincingly varied output and one that keeps emitting the same few high-frequency fragments.
algorithms.citation: Kneser & Ney, Improved backing-off for m-gram language modeling, ICASSP 1995, 181–184

algorithms.name: Social force model
algorithms.summary: Pedestrians as particles under fictitious social forces — a drive toward the goal, repulsion from others and walls.
algorithms.eli5: Model a pedestrian as though attractive and repulsive forces acted on them: drawn towards their destination, pushed away from other people and from walls. Sum the forces and take a step. Crowds jam in doorways and self-organise into lanes in corridors without any rule saying so.
algorithms.description: Treat each pedestrian as a point mass under three kinds of force. An acceleration term drives them toward their desired velocity — the direction and speed they want to be going. Repulsive terms push them away from other pedestrians and from walls, falling off exponentially with distance and weighted by whether the obstacle is in front of them. Attractive terms pull toward things they want to approach. Integrate and crowds emerge: lanes form spontaneously in bidirectional flow, arch-shaped jams appear at doorways, and at high density the model reproduces the faster-is-slower effect where increasing individual urgency reduces total throughput. That last result is why the model is used seriously for evacuation planning and venue design rather than just for making crowds look busy.
algorithms.citation: Helbing & Molnár, Social force model for pedestrian dynamics, Physical Review E 51(5), 4282–4286

algorithms.name: Straight skeleton
algorithms.authors: Oswin Aichholzer, Franz Aurenhammer, David Alberts, Bernd Gärtner
algorithms.summary: Shrink a polygon by moving every edge inward at constant speed; the traces of the vertices form the skeleton. Solves roofs from a footprint.
algorithms.eli5: Shrink a shape by moving every wall inward at the same speed simultaneously. The corners trace out lines as they move, and those lines are the skeleton — exactly where the ridges and valleys of a roof would fall if you roofed that outline.
algorithms.description: Move every edge of the polygon inward, parallel to itself, at the same constant speed. Each vertex travels along its angle bisector, and the paths those vertices trace out are the straight skeleton. Two things interrupt the shrinking: an edge event, where an edge collapses to zero length and its neighbours become adjacent, and a split event, where a reflex vertex crashes into an opposite edge and cuts the polygon in two. Unlike the medial axis it contains only straight segments, never arcs. Its use in architecture falls straight out of the definition: if you lift the shrinking wavefront vertically at a constant rate, the surface swept is a roof of uniform pitch, so hip and gable roofs come free from the building footprint.
algorithms.citation: A novel type of skeleton for polygons, J. Universal Computer Science 1(12), 752–761

algorithms.name: Open L-systems
algorithms.summary: L-systems extended with bidirectional information exchange with the environment, so growth responds to light, space and competition.
algorithms.eli5: The plant above is blind: its branches grow through walls and through each other. Here the pen can pause and ask questions. Is there light at this position? Is a branch already here? A separate program modelling the environment answers, and the plant grows around what it finds.
algorithms.description: Ordinary L-systems are closed — the rules cannot see anything outside the string, which is why naive trees grow branches through each other and through the trunk. Open L-systems add query modules: special symbols that the turtle interpretation writes environmental data into, such as the light reaching that position or whether the space is already occupied. An external environment program reads the plant's current geometry, computes the answers, and writes them back; the next derivation step then has rules that branch on those values. Growth becomes a conversation rather than a monologue, which is what makes shade avoidance, pruning and competition between neighbouring plants expressible at all.
algorithms.citation: Visual Models of Plants Interacting with Their Environment, SIGGRAPH '96

algorithms.name: Sphere tracing
algorithms.summary: March along a ray in steps as long as the distance field allows. The reason SDF scenes can be rendered without geometry.
algorithms.eli5: You are advancing along a ray looking for the first surface, in a scene where you can always ask how far away the nearest surface is. So ask, then advance exactly that distance — you cannot have passed through anything, because nothing was closer. Ask again. Near a surface the steps shrink and the process converges.
algorithms.description: Given a function returning a lower bound on the distance to the nearest surface, the ray can be advanced by that distance with no risk of stepping through anything: the sphere of that radius is provably empty. Iterating converges geometrically on the first intersection, and terminates when the distance drops below a threshold or the ray leaves the scene. The consequences are what made the technique matter. Any shape you can write a distance bound for is renderable with no tessellation, no acceleration structure and no memory, so booleans, blends, infinite repetition by taking coordinates modulo a period, and domain distortions all become one-line changes. Normals come free from the field's gradient, and ambient occlusion and soft shadows come nearly free from sampling the field itself. Its costs are equally characteristic: grazing rays crawl, because each step is small while the surface stays close, and any operation that breaks the distance bound — non-uniform scaling, cheap smooth-minimum blends — makes the marcher overshoot and produce holes.
algorithms.citation: Hart, Sphere tracing: a geometric method for the antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces, The Visual Computer 12(10), 527–545

algorithms.name: Wilson's algorithm
algorithms.summary: Generates a uniformly random spanning tree by loop-erased random walks. Every possible maze equally likely.
algorithms.eli5: Most maze methods are biased: they produce some shapes more often than others. This one is not. Take a cell not yet in the maze, walk at random erasing your own loops whenever you cross your path, and when you finally reach the maze, carve the walk you were left holding.
algorithms.description: Pick any vertex and call it the tree. Then repeatedly: choose a vertex not yet in the tree and random-walk from it, erasing loops as they form — if the walk revisits its own path, cut out the loop and carry on from that point. When the walk finally touches the tree, add the whole loop-erased path to it. Repeat until every vertex is in. The result is drawn uniformly from all spanning trees of the graph, which matters because the popular alternatives are biased: recursive backtracker produces long snaking corridors with few junctions, Prim's produces bushy short-branched ones, and neither samples the space of mazes evenly. Wilson's is slower to start — early walks wander a long time before finding the small tree — but it is the only simple algorithm that is genuinely unbiased.
algorithms.citation: Generating random spanning trees more quickly than the cover time, Proc. 28th ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing, 296–303

algorithms.name: Worley / cellular noise
algorithms.summary: Distance to the nth nearest feature point. F1 and F2 give cells, cracks, scales and caustics. Written explicitly as a complement to Perlin noise.
algorithms.eli5: Scatter points. For any position, return the distance to the nearest one. The result is a field of cells with a ridge wherever two points are equally close — the pattern of cracked mud, stone, or the skin of an orange.
algorithms.description: Scatter feature points through space — in practice one or a few per grid cell, jittered, so only the 27 neighbouring cells need checking. For a sample point, compute the sorted distances to nearby features: F1 is the nearest, F2 the second nearest. F1 alone gives rounded cell blobs that darken toward each seed. F2 minus F1 is near zero exactly on the boundary between two cells, so it draws the cracks — which is where flagstones, scales, dried mud and crackle come from. Changing the distance metric changes the cell shape: Euclidean gives organic cells, Manhattan and Chebyshev give angular, crystalline ones.
algorithms.citation: A Cellular Texture Basis Function, SIGGRAPH '96, 291–294

algorithms.name: D-infinity flow routing
algorithms.summary: Give each cell a continuous downslope angle and split its water between the two neighbours either side of it.
algorithms.eli5: Sending all the water to one of eight neighbours forces every stream onto a compass direction, so hillsides end up striped with parallel single-cell lines. Instead, compute the true downhill direction as a continuous angle and divide the water between the two neighbours it falls between, in proportion. Flow can now spread and fan the way it actually does.
algorithms.description: Fit eight triangular facets to each cell and its neighbours, take the steepest downslope direction across all of them as a continuous angle, then apportion flow between the two cardinal or diagonal neighbours bracketing that angle in proportion to the angular distance. The result keeps the single-direction methods' ability to converge into channels while allowing divergence on hillslopes and fans, which is what D8 structurally cannot do — its artefact is parallel single-cell flow lines on any planar slope. Accumulation becomes a weighted sum over a directed acyclic graph rather than a tree, so it still computes in one topological pass. For terrain generation the difference shows exactly where it matters most: alluvial fans, deltas, braided channels and the broad wetted areas that make a valley floor read as a floodplain rather than as a single scratched line.
algorithms.citation: Tarboton, A new method for the determination of flow directions and upslope areas in grid digital elevation models, Water Resources Research 33(2), 309–319

algorithms.name: Quadric error metric decimation
algorithms.summary: Collapse the edge whose removal moves the surface least, measured by a per-vertex quadratic form. The standard LOD algorithm.
algorithms.eli5: To simplify a surface, merge two nearby vertices into one. But which pair, and where should the merged vertex go? Give every vertex a small quadratic form recording how much error placing it anywhere would cause. Add the two forms, solve for the position of least error, and always merge whichever pair is cheapest.
algorithms.description: Each vertex carries a 4×4 symmetric matrix — the sum of outer products of the plane equations of its incident faces — which evaluates, for any candidate position, the total squared distance to those original planes. Collapsing an edge adds the two matrices, and minimising the resulting quadratic is a small linear solve giving both the optimal merged position and the error incurred. Put every candidate collapse in a priority queue by that error, pop the cheapest, collapse, and update the affected neighbours. Because the error is accumulated rather than recomputed against the original mesh, cost stays low while quality stays high, and the same formulation extends to preserving colour and UVs by widening the quadric. This is what almost every automatic LOD chain, mesh budget tool and game-engine importer runs, which makes it the algorithm that decides what generated geometry looks like at distance — and its known failure mode is that it will happily collapse a thin feature that lies close to its own plane.
algorithms.citation: Garland & Heckbert, Surface simplification using quadric error metrics, SIGGRAPH 97, 209–216

algorithms.name: Exact geometric predicates
algorithms.summary: Adaptive-precision arithmetic that makes orientation and in-circle tests exact, so boolean and meshing code stops crashing.
algorithms.eli5: Every geometric algorithm rests on questions such as "is this point left of that line?". With ordinary floating-point arithmetic the answer is occasionally wrong by a hair, and a single wrong answer makes the whole algorithm produce nonsense. The remedy is arithmetic that is exact when it needs to be, and that can determine cheaply when that is.
algorithms.description: Mesh booleans, Delaunay triangulation and BSP construction all rest on two questions: which side of a plane is this point on, and is this point inside that circumsphere. Both are determinant signs, and in floating point a near-degenerate input can return the wrong sign — producing not a slightly wrong answer but an inconsistent topology, which is why boolean modelling has a reputation for fragility. Shewchuk's method computes these predicates exactly using expansions of floating-point values, and does so adaptively: compute a fast approximate result first with an error bound, and only escalate to more precision when the bound cannot decide the sign. In the overwhelming majority of cases the cheap path suffices, so exactness costs almost nothing on average. This is the substrate under CGAL, Triangle and most robust CSG in production.
algorithms.citation: Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates, Discrete & Computational Geometry 18(3), 305–363

algorithms.name: Bilateral filter
algorithms.summary: Blur, but only average samples that are similar in value as well as close in space. Smooths without crossing edges.
algorithms.eli5: An ordinary blur smears across every boundary, so sharp edges soften. Add one rule: only include a neighbour in the average if its value is also close to yours. Flat areas smooth out and edges survive, because values on the far side of an edge never contribute.
algorithms.description: Multiply the usual spatial weight by a second weight based on how different the neighbour's value is from the centre's, and normalise. Two parameters — a spatial radius and a value tolerance — control how far it looks and how much difference it will tolerate. The result is that gradients are smoothed while steps survive, which is why it underlies denoising, tone mapping, cartoon shading and the "detail layer" split used throughout texture authoring: bilateral-filter a heightfield, subtract, and you have separated the large forms from the fine grain without the halos a Gaussian split produces. It is not separable and naively costs O(r²) per pixel, which drove a decade of accelerations — the bilateral grid, the permutohedral lattice, and the guided filter, which achieves the same edge-aware behaviour in linear time. Its known artefact is gradient reversal near strong edges, visible as a thin halo when the detail layer is amplified.
algorithms.citation: Tomasi & Manduchi, Bilateral filtering for gray and color images, ICCV 1998, 839–846

algorithms.name: Mersenne Twister
algorithms.summary: Period 2^19937−1 and 623-dimensional equidistribution from 624 words of state. The default PRNG almost everywhere.
algorithms.eli5: A generator holding 624 numbers as state and mixing them with shifts and exclusive-ors. It will not repeat for an extraordinarily long time and passes the statistical tests that mattered in 1998. Large, slow to initialise, and not to be used anywhere someone has an incentive to predict it.
algorithms.description: A twisted generalised feedback shift register. State is 624 32-bit words; each step combines two words far apart in the array with a bit-mixing 'twist' matrix, then passes the result through a tempering transform of shifts and masks to flatten the output distribution. The period is a Mersenne prime, 2^19937−1, and it is provably equidistributed in up to 623 dimensions at 32-bit precision — meaning consecutive outputs cover high-dimensional space uniformly, which is the property Monte Carlo integration actually needs. Its weaknesses are practical rather than statistical: 2.5 KB of state is large, recovering from a poor seed takes a long time, and observing 624 outputs reveals the entire internal state, so it is unsuitable anywhere unpredictability matters.
algorithms.citation: Mersenne Twister: A 623-dimensionally equidistributed uniform pseudo-random number generator, ACM Trans. Modeling and Computer Simulation 8(1), 3–30

algorithms.name: Surface nets
algorithms.summary: One vertex per surface-crossing cell, relaxed to smooth the mesh while constrained to stay inside its own cell. The first dual contouring method.
algorithms.eli5: Instead of cutting triangles inside each cube, place a single vertex in every cube the surface passes through, then move each vertex towards where the surface actually crosses. Connect the vertices of adjacent cubes into quads. Far fewer and much better-shaped polygons, at the cost of softening every corner.
algorithms.description: Where marching cubes places vertices on cube edges, surface nets places exactly one vertex inside each cube that the surface passes through, and connects vertices in neighbouring cubes to form quads — the dual arrangement. The vertex positions are then relaxed iteratively, each one pulled toward the average of its linked neighbours to smooth the mesh, but clamped so it can never leave its original cube. That constraint is what stops the smoothing from shrinking the model away.
