This is the bridge between the field and SDF representations: any mask, silhouette or voxelisation becomes a signed distance function by running it once on the inside and once on the outside. Also the standard preprocessing step for erosion masks, flow-cost fields and dilation by an exact radius.
algorithms.citation: Felzenszwalb & Huttenlocher, Distance transforms of sampled functions, Theory of Computing 8, 415–428 (2012); first circulated as Cornell TR2004-1963

algorithms.name: Variational autoencoder
algorithms.summary: An autoencoder whose latent space is regularised to a known distribution, so you can sample from it.
algorithms.eli5: Compress each training image to a handful of numbers, and train a second network to reconstruct the image from them. Constrain the compressed representations to cluster into one well-behaved region, and then any point you choose in that region — including points no real image occupied — reconstructs into something plausible.
algorithms.description: A plain autoencoder compresses inputs to a latent code and reconstructs them, but the latent space is full of holes — sample a random point and you get garbage. A VAE encodes to a *distribution* rather than a point, samples from it during training via the reparameterisation trick (so gradients still flow), and adds a KL term pulling every encoded distribution toward a standard Gaussian. That regularisation is what makes the space continuous and samplable: draw any point from the prior and the decoder produces something plausible, and interpolating between two codes traverses meaningful intermediates. For generation this is the difference between compression and a generative model. Its characteristic weakness is blur — the reconstruction objective averages over plausible outputs, which is precisely what GANs avoid and diffusion models fix differently.
algorithms.citation: Kingma & Welling, Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes, arXiv:1312.6114 (ICLR 2014)

algorithms.name: Generative adversarial network
algorithms.summary: A generator and a discriminator trained against each other. The loss function is a second network.
algorithms.eli5: Two networks in opposition. One produces images; the other tries to distinguish produced images from real ones. Each improves because the other does, and when the discriminator can no longer tell, the generator is producing convincing images. Notoriously unstable, because either side can win.
algorithms.description: Two networks in a minimax game. The generator maps noise to samples; the discriminator tries to tell generated samples from real ones; the generator is trained to fool it. Neither has an explicit likelihood — the learning signal is entirely the discriminator's gradient, which means the objective adapts as the generator improves rather than being fixed in advance. This is why GAN output is sharp where VAE output is blurry: nothing is averaging over plausible answers, only escaping detection. The corresponding difficulty is that a minimax game need not converge, and the classic failure is mode collapse, where the generator finds one convincing output and abandons variety entirely — which for content generation is the worst possible failure, since variety was the point.
algorithms.citation: Goodfellow et al., Generative Adversarial Networks, NeurIPS 2014, arXiv:1406.2661

algorithms.name: PCG
algorithms.summary: A linear congruential generator with a permuted output. Small state, fast, statistically strong, and streamable.
algorithms.eli5: Take a well-understood but visibly patterned generator, then conceal the pattern by scrambling its output — including using part of the internal state to decide how to scramble. Small, fast, statistically strong, and able to provide fully independent streams, which matters when a world is generated in parallel.
algorithms.description: Linear congruential generators are fast and tiny but notoriously weak — their low bits are barely random and their outputs fall on lattice planes. PCG keeps the LCG as the state transition and fixes the output instead, applying a permutation whose parameters are themselves drawn from the high bits of the state: a variable rotation or xorshift chosen by the number it is scrambling. That self-referential step destroys the lattice structure while adding a few instructions. The result passes TestU01's BigCrush on 64 bits of state, where Mersenne Twister needs 20,000. For procedural work the practically important features are cheap seeding, multiple independent streams from the same seed, and the ability to jump ahead — which is what makes deterministic per-chunk sub-seeding of infinite worlds tractable.
algorithms.citation: PCG: A Family of Simple Fast Space-Efficient Statistically Good Algorithms for Random Number Generation, Harvey Mudd College TR HMC-CS-2014-0905

algorithms.name: Priority-flood depression filling
algorithms.authors: Richard Barnes, Clarence Lehman, David Mulla
algorithms.summary: Flood the terrain inwards from its edges using a priority queue. Fills every pit optimally, in one pass.
algorithms.eli5: Real terrain is full of small depressions, and water routed across it becomes trapped in them instead of reaching the sea. So flood inward from the boundary, always expanding from the lowest cell reachable so far, and raise any cell below the level that reached it. Every depression fills to its own outlet and no further, in a single traversal.
algorithms.description: Push all the boundary cells into a priority queue keyed by elevation. Repeatedly pop the lowest, and for each unvisited neighbour, raise it to at least the popped cell's elevation before pushing it. Because you always expand from the lowest available point, the water level at which each cell is reached is exactly the lowest possible spill elevation for that cell, so every depression is filled to its own outlet and no further — provably optimal, and in a single traversal. Cost is O(n) for integer elevations, using a radix-style queue, and O(n log n) for floating point; the pseudocode is under twenty lines. This is the precondition step for the rest of hydrology, because D8 routing on unfilled data terminates in local pits and produces drainage that never reaches an outlet. Variants either fill flat, which leaves ambiguous plateaus, or add an epsilon gradient towards the outlet so that routing across the filled region still has a direction.
algorithms.citation: Barnes, Lehman & Mulla, Priority-flood: an optimal depression-filling and watershed-labeling algorithm for digital elevation models, Computers & Geosciences 62, 117–127

algorithms.name: SplitMix
algorithms.authors: Guy L. Steele Jr., Doug Lea, Christine H. Flood
algorithms.summary: A splittable generator: derive independent child streams from a parent without coordination.
algorithms.eli5: Rather than stepping a generator along a chain, simply count upwards and scramble the counter thoroughly. Because there is no chain, an independent generator can be split off at any point, which is what per-object and parallel generation require. Also the standard way to expand one seed into good initial state for something else.
algorithms.description: Most generators produce one sequence, which makes parallel and hierarchical generation awkward — two threads sharing a generator must synchronise, and two chunks of a world drawing from the same stream become order-dependent. SplitMix adds a split operation that derives a fresh, statistically independent generator from an existing one, with no shared state afterwards. Internally it is a counter advanced by a fixed odd increment, passed through a strong bit-mixing finaliser (MurmurHash3's); splitting picks a new increment. It costs about nine operations per 64 bits. For procedural generation this is the principled answer to per-chunk sub-seeding: instead of hashing coordinates into a seed and hoping, you split the world generator per chunk and get provable independence and reproducibility regardless of what order chunks are visited.
algorithms.citation: Steele, Lea & Flood, Fast splittable pseudorandom number generators, OOPSLA 2014

algorithms.name: Field-aligned quad remeshing
algorithms.authors: Wenzel Jakob, Marco Tarini, Daniele Panozzo, Olga Sorkine-Hornung
algorithms.summary: Smooth an orientation field and a position field over a surface, then read a clean quad mesh straight off them.
algorithms.eli5: To cover a surface in a tidy grid of quads you first need agreement, everywhere on the surface, about which direction counts as "along". So let each point negotiate with its neighbours until the directions align with the surface's natural curvature. Then do the same for where the grid lines fall. The quads are where the lines cross.
algorithms.description: Two smoothing problems, solved in sequence over the surface. First an orientation field: each point holds a cross of directions, and neighbouring points are pulled towards agreement modulo 90°, so the field follows principal curvature and folds gracefully around the singular points a closed surface forces to exist. Then a position field: each point holds a candidate lattice offset, again smoothed towards local agreement, which fixes where the grid lines fall. Extracting the mesh is then a local operation. The formulation is entirely local and parallel, needs no global parameterisation, and runs interactively on meshes with millions of triangles, which is what separated it from the earlier global-optimisation approaches. For generation, this is the step that turns something built by marching cubes or sculpted from an SDF into geometry that can be subdivided, UV-mapped and animated — the "retopology" the catalogue lists as an entry with no method attached.
algorithms.citation: Jakob, Tarini, Panozzo & Sorkine-Hornung, Instant field-aligned meshes, ACM TOG 34(6) (SIGGRAPH Asia 2015)

algorithms.name: MAP-Elites
algorithms.summary: Keep the best solution found in every cell of a feature grid, not the single best overall. Returns a diverse archive.
algorithms.eli5: Define a grid whose axes are the properties you want variety in — height, mass, difficulty. Every candidate falls into one cell, and each cell retains only its own best. What you have at the end is not a single winner but a catalogue of the best example of each kind, which is usually what a generator was wanted for.
algorithms.description: Choose a small number of interesting features — for a creature, perhaps height and mass; for a level, perhaps corridor density and difficulty — and discretise that space into a grid. Maintain one elite per cell: the highest-performing solution found so far with those feature values. Each iteration, pick a random elite, mutate it, evaluate the child, and place it in whichever cell its features fall into, keeping it only if it beats the current occupant. The output is not one answer but a filled map showing the best achievable performance at every combination of features, which is far more useful for content than a single optimum — it tells you what the space *can* produce, and it is the practical answer to the expressive-range problem the catalogue's own pitfalls page raises. Elites also act as stepping stones for each other, so it often finds better global optima than objective-driven search.
algorithms.citation: Mouret & Clune, Illuminating search spaces by mapping elites, arXiv:1504.04909

algorithms.name: SMPL
algorithms.authors: Matthew Loper, Naureen Mahmood, Javier Romero, Gerard Pons-Moll, Michael Black
algorithms.summary: A learned body model where shape, pose and pose-dependent deformation are all fitted from scans rather than authored.
algorithms.eli5: A body model with two independent sets of parameters: one for the shape of the person, one for the pose of their joints. The important part is that it also learned how the surface should deform in each pose, so a raised arm produces a correct bulge rather than the pinched crease a plain skeleton gives.
algorithms.description: A vertex-based body model driven by a standard skeleton, but with every component learned from thousands of registered scans rather than sculpted: the rest-pose template, the blend weights, identity blend shapes capturing how bodies differ, pose blend shapes capturing how flesh deforms as joints bend, and a regressor predicting joint locations from surface shape. The pose blend shapes are the important part — they fix the candy-wrapper collapse and volume loss that plain linear blend skinning produces at elbows and shoulders, by learning the corrective deformation instead of hand-rigging it. Because the whole thing stays a linear model with a skeleton, it drops into existing engines and renderers unchanged, which is why it became the standard body representation for both graphics and computer vision.
algorithms.citation: Loper et al., SMPL: A Skinned Multi-Person Linear Model, ACM TOG 34(6) (SIGGRAPH Asia 2015)

algorithms.name: Tracery
algorithms.authors: Kate Compton, Ben Kybartas, Michael Mateas
algorithms.summary: A minimal JSON grammar for generative text, designed so non-programmers can author generators.
algorithms.eli5: Templates with slots, where any slot may contain another template. "The #adjective# #animal# ate my #food#", with a list of options for each. It is the simplest method in this catalogue, which is exactly why so many text-generating bots are built from it.
algorithms.description: A Tracery grammar is a JSON object mapping symbol names to arrays of expansions, where an expansion may reference other symbols in braces. Expand the start symbol recursively, choosing randomly among alternatives, and you get a sentence. That is deliberately almost nothing — the contribution is not the formalism, which is a context-free grammar, but the design decisions around authorability: additive authoring so a grammar stays runnable while half-written, modular grammars that can be shared and combined, and data portability so a grammar is a file rather than a program. It powered a generation of Twitter bots and is the reason procedural text became accessible to writers rather than only programmers. Compton's accompanying framing of generativity is the same body of thought as the 10,000 bowls of oatmeal problem in this catalogue's pitfalls.
algorithms.citation: Compton, Kybartas & Mateas, Tracery: An Author-Focused Generative Text Tool, ICIDS 2015

algorithms.name: Wave Function Collapse
algorithms.summary: Learn adjacency from one example, then collapse the lowest-entropy cell and propagate. Forked over a thousand times.
algorithms.eli5: Every cell begins able to hold any tile. Pick the cell with the fewest remaining options, choose one of them, and propagate the consequences: its neighbours lose the tiles that no longer fit, which constrains their neighbours in turn. Continue until every cell is decided.
algorithms.description: Every output cell starts in superposition — a set containing every tile that could legally go there. Repeatedly: find the cell with the fewest remaining options (lowest entropy), pick one of its options at random weighted by how often that tile appeared in the example, and then propagate. Propagation removes from each neighbour any option that has no legal partner in the collapsed cell, and any removal cascades onward until nothing changes. Repeat until every cell is decided. The adjacency rules themselves are learned by sliding an N×N window over the example image and recording which patterns can overlap. Its well-known failure is contradiction — a cell whose options all get eliminated — which requires backtracking or a full restart, and it has no notion of global properties, so it cannot tell whether the level it produced is completable.
algorithms.citation: mxgmn/WaveFunctionCollapse, released 2016; related to Merrell's model synthesis

algorithms.name: FLAME
algorithms.authors: Tianye Li, Timo Bolkart, Michael Black, Hao Li, Javier Romero
algorithms.summary: A head model with articulated jaw, neck and eyes plus learned pose and expression correctives. SMPL for faces.
algorithms.eli5: The head equivalent, separated three ways: who the person is, what the jaw and neck are doing, and what expression is being made. Because the three are independent, one person's smile can be applied to another person's face without turning them into that other person.
algorithms.description: Where Blanz and Vetter's morphable model captured a static face, FLAME adds articulation. It combines a linear identity shape space learned from around 3,800 head scans with an actual skeleton — jaw, neck and eyeballs — plus pose-dependent corrective blendshapes that fix the deformation errors linear blend skinning introduces around a rotating jaw, and a separate expression space learned from 4D sequences rather than static poses. That separation matters: identity, pose and expression become independent axes, so you can put any expression on any face at any head angle without them interfering. It is explicitly the face analogue of SMPL, by an overlapping group, and it is the base model under a large share of current avatar and talking-head work.
algorithms.citation: Li, Bolkart, Black, Li & Romero, Learning a model of facial shape and expression from 4D scans, ACM TOG 36(6) (SIGGRAPH Asia 2017)

algorithms.name: Transformer
algorithms.authors: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin
algorithms.summary: Sequence modelling by attention alone: every position looks directly at every other. No recurrence, so it parallelises.
algorithms.eli5: Earlier sequence models read one item at a time, carrying a running summary, so distant items faded and nothing could be processed in parallel. Here every position can attend directly to every other and decide for itself which matter. Nothing needs remembering because everything is still in view, and every position can be processed simultaneously — which is what made scale possible.
algorithms.description: Each position produces a query, a key and a value; attention weights are the softmax of query-key products, and the output is the weighted sum of values. Multiple heads let different relationships be attended to at once, and since the mechanism is order-blind, positional encodings are added to the inputs. Stacking these with feed-forward layers, residual connections and layer normalisation gives a model whose path length between any two positions is one, which is what fixed the long-range degradation of recurrent models — and, more consequentially, whose training parallelises across the whole sequence instead of stepping through it. That single property is what made scale possible and therefore what the entire subsequent generative-model era rests on. Cost is the trade: attention is quadratic in sequence length. For generation the reach is far past text — the same architecture generates music as token sequences, level layouts as tile sequences, meshes as face sequences, and is the denoising backbone in most current image diffusion models.
algorithms.citation: Vaswani et al., Attention is all you need, NeurIPS 2017

algorithms.name: Adjoint-gradient inverse design
algorithms.authors: Sean Molesky, Zin Lin, Alexander Piggott, Weiliang Jin, Jelena Vučković, Alejandro Rodriguez
algorithms.summary: Get the gradient with respect to millions of design variables from two simulations, not millions, by solving the problem backwards.
algorithms.eli5: You want to know how each of a million design variables affects the result. Adjusting each and re-running the simulation would take a million simulations. Instead, run the simulation once forwards and a related problem once backwards, and combine the two — which gives the effect of every variable for the cost of two runs. That single fact is why these geometries look like nothing a person would draw.
algorithms.description: For an objective depending on the solution of a linear physical system, the derivative with respect to every design variable can be assembled from the forward solution and the solution of one adjoint system — the transpose problem driven by the objective's sensitivity. Two solves total, regardless of whether there are ten design variables or ten million. That single fact is what makes it possible to optimise every voxel of a photonic device, an antenna or a heat exchanger, and it is why the resulting geometries look nothing like human designs: no designer was ever able to explore that space. Practically the loop is the same as SIMP's — density variables, a filter for minimum feature size, projection towards binary — with a wave or transport simulation in place of the finite-element structural solve, and fabrication constraints are the hard part rather than the optimisation. This review is the standard entry point and the source of the term as used in nanophotonics.
algorithms.citation: Molesky, Lin, Piggott, Jin, Vučković & Rodriguez, Inverse design in nanophotonics, Nature Photonics 12, 659–670

algorithms.name: Histogram-preserving blending
algorithms.summary: Infinite non-repeating texture from one example, by blending three patches on a triangle lattice without losing contrast.
algorithms.eli5: Cross-fading two texture tiles by simple averaging leaves both washed out, because averaging independent values reduces their spread. The fix: transform each texture into a standard distribution first, average in that space, then transform back. Contrast survives the blend.
algorithms.description: Partition the output over an equilateral triangle lattice — the same lattice simplex noise uses — and give every vertex a random offset into the example texture. Any output point falls inside one triangle, so it blends the three patches belonging to that triangle's vertices, weighted by barycentric coordinates. The problem is that averaging several patches is averaging random variables, which shrinks variance and turns crisp granite into grey mush. The fix is to first transform the input through a histogram transformation into a Gaussian distribution, do the blending there where averaging behaves predictably, then apply the inverse transformation to restore the original histogram exactly. Contrast survives, no seam is visible, and the result is over twenty times faster than comparable by-example noise.
algorithms.citation: High-Performance By-Example Noise using a Histogram-Preserving Blending Operator, Proc. ACM CGIT / HPG 2018

algorithms.name: xoshiro / xoroshiro
algorithms.summary: Modern xorshift descendants: shift, rotate, XOR, plus a scrambler on the output. Very fast, small state.
algorithms.eli5: A small amount of state, shifted and rotated a few times per value, with the state update deliberately separated from the output scrambling. Currently the sensible default for anything that is not cryptography: faster than the Mersenne Twister, a fraction of the size, and it passes harder tests.
algorithms.description: Plain xorshift is linear over GF(2), which shows up as failures in tests sensitive to linear structure — notably the low bits and binary-rank tests. The xoshiro and xoroshiro families keep a fast linear state transition built from xor, shift and rotate, but pass the output through a non-linear scrambler before returning it: multiplication for the ** variants, addition for the + variants. This keeps the throughput of xorshift while fixing its statistical weaknesses, in 128 or 256 bits of state rather than Mersenne Twister's 2.5 KB. They also provide jump functions that advance the state by a huge fixed distance, giving non-overlapping streams for parallel work. Note the + variants still have weak low bits by design and are intended for producing floats, not integers.
algorithms.citation: Blackman & Vigna, Scrambled linear pseudorandom number generators, ACM TOMS 47(4), 2021; see prng.di.unimi.it

algorithms.name: CP-SAT
algorithms.authors: Google OR-Tools team (Laurent Perron et al.)
algorithms.summary: A lazy clause generation solver combining constraint propagation with SAT clause learning. The practical industrial default.
algorithms.eli5: Translate a scheduling problem into pure true-or-false clauses and hand it to machinery that is remarkably good at true-or-false. Then run several different search strategies in parallel and let them share the facts they learn. Inelegant, and it wins competitions.
algorithms.description: Constraint programming propagates well but backtracks blindly; SAT learns from every failure but expresses arithmetic awkwardly. CP-SAT is a lazy clause generation solver that runs both: high-level constraints — all-different, cumulative resource, interval scheduling — propagate as in CP, but every propagation records a clausal explanation, so when a conflict occurs the SAT engine can learn a clause and backjump rather than merely undoing the last decision. It also runs a portfolio of strategies in parallel and shares learned clauses between them. For generation the significance is practical rather than theoretical: this is the solver most rostering, timetabling and packing actually runs on, it is free, and its model API is close enough to how you would state the problem in English that it removes most of the reason to hand-roll a search.
algorithms.citation: Google OR-Tools CP-SAT solver. Documented in the OR-Tools repository and Perron's talks rather than a single paper.

algorithms.name: Procedural tectonic planets
algorithms.authors: Yann Cortial, Adrien Peytavie, Eric Galin, Eric Guérin
algorithms.summary: Approximates plate subduction and collision to deform a planetary lithosphere into continents, ridges and mountain ranges.
algorithms.eli5: Divide a planet's crust into a few dozen rigid plates and move them. Where two collide, raise mountains; where they separate, open an ocean; where one descends beneath another, cut a trench and place a chain of volcanoes. Run it for a few hundred million years and the continents look as though they have a history, because they do.
algorithms.description: Represent the crust as a set of moving plates on a sphere, each tagged continental or oceanic and carrying a velocity. Where two plates converge, the outcome depends on the pair: oceanic beneath continental subducts and raises a coastal range, continental against continental thickens the crust into a large mountain belt, oceanic against oceanic produces island arcs. Where plates diverge, new oceanic crust is created at the ridge. Crucially the paper approximates these outcomes with procedural rules rather than integrating the physics, explicitly to avoid the cost of a real geodynamic simulation — so it sits partway along the axis between imitating an outcome and deriving one. The large-scale result is then amplified with noise or real elevation data for detail.
algorithms.citation: Procedural Tectonic Planets, Computer Graphics Forum 38(2) / Eurographics 2019

algorithms.name: Denoising diffusion (DDPM)
algorithms.authors: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain, Pieter Abbeel
algorithms.summary: Learn to reverse a gradual noising process. Generate by starting from noise and denoising step by step.
algorithms.eli5: Take an image and add a small amount of noise. Repeat a thousand times until nothing but noise remains. Now train a network to undo a single one of those steps. Run the undoing a thousand times starting from fresh noise, and an image that never existed comes out.
algorithms.description: Define a fixed forward process that adds a little Gaussian noise at each of many steps until the data becomes pure noise. Then train a network to predict the noise that was added at a given step, which is equivalent to learning the reverse process. Generation runs the reverse chain: start from noise and denoise repeatedly. The reason this beats GANs on stability is that the objective is a plain regression loss on noise prediction — no adversary, no minimax, no mode collapse, and the model is forced to cover the whole distribution rather than find one convincing corner. The cost is sampling speed, since generation needs many network evaluations rather than one, which is what every subsequent sampler and distillation method attacks. This is the paper the current generation of image, video, motion and molecule models descends from.
algorithms.citation: Ho, Jain & Abbeel, Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models, NeurIPS 2020

algorithms.name: Neural radiance fields
algorithms.authors: Ben Mildenhall, Pratul Srinivasan, Matthew Tancik, Jonathan Barron, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Ren Ng
algorithms.summary: Fit a small network mapping position and view direction to colour and density. Render by volume raymarching.
algorithms.eli5: Take a few dozen photographs of a subject from different angles. Train a network to answer one question: at this point in space, viewed from this direction, what colour is it and how opaque? Integrating those answers along each line of sight renders photographs from viewpoints nobody occupied.
algorithms.description: The scene is not a mesh or a voxel grid but the weights of a small multilayer perceptron that maps a 5D input — position plus viewing direction — to a colour and a volume density. Render by marching rays through it and compositing samples, which is differentiable, so the network can be fitted by gradient descent directly against a set of photographs. Two details do most of the work: positional encoding, projecting the input coordinates onto a bank of sinusoids of increasing frequency, because networks otherwise cannot represent high-frequency detail; and view-dependent colour, which is what captures specularity and gloss. The consequence for this catalogue is a genuinely new representation class — scenes as learned functions, alongside meshes, SDFs and point clouds.
algorithms.citation: Mildenhall et al., NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis, ECCV 2020, arXiv:2003.08934

algorithms.name: Neural cellular automata
algorithms.authors: Alexander Mordvintsev, Ettore Randazzo, Eyvind Niklasson, Michael Levin
algorithms.summary: Replace a cellular automaton's hand-written rule with a small trained network. The rule is learned, and the result regenerates when damaged.
algorithms.eli5: A cellular automaton needs someone to invent its rule. Here the rule is a small neural network instead, trained so that running it from a single seed cell produces a target image. What comes back is a rule rather than a picture — and because it was trained to keep producing the image, it regrows the missing part when you cut a piece away.
algorithms.description: Each cell holds a small vector of channels, four of them visible as colour and alpha and the rest hidden state. The update is a fixed perception step — the cell's own state plus Sobel gradients of its neighbourhood — followed by a tiny multilayer network shared by every cell, applied stochastically so cells do not update in lockstep. Training backpropagates through many update steps towards a target image, with damaged states injected into the training pool so that persistence and regeneration are learned rather than hoped for. The result is a rule, not a picture: it is local, parallel, has no coordinate system, and grows to the target from a seed then holds it stably. This is the bridge between the `ca` and `ml` concepts and a genuinely different point on the trade-off, because the model is a few thousand parameters rather than a few hundred million, and its behaviour — self-repair without any global plan — is the property hand-written automata almost never have.
algorithms.citation: Mordvintsev, Randazzo, Niklasson & Levin, Growing Neural Cellular Automata, Distill, 2020. doi:10.23915/distill.00023

algorithms.name: Oklab
algorithms.summary: A perceptual space fitted for hue uniformity and cheap to compute. Now the default for interpolation on the web.
algorithms.eli5: CIELAB is good but its hues drift: blend blue with white in it and the midpoint turns purple. This space was fitted specifically so that blending two colours preserves the hue you would expect, and so that lightness changes do not shift apparent hue. The whole conversion is two matrix multiplications and a cube root, which is cheap enough to run in a shader.
algorithms.description: Built by optimising a simple pipeline — a matrix into an LMS-like cone space, a cube root, then a second matrix into opponent axes — against datasets of perceived hue and lightness, with the explicit design goal of hue linearity rather than of minimal average error. The consequence is the behaviour that matters for generation: gradients keep their hue instead of drifting through purple, and lightness changes do not shift apparent hue, so a tint and shade scale generated by moving L alone stays recognisably the same colour. Its cheapness is the other half of the story — no white-point adaptation, no piecewise branches, so it fits in a fragment shader and in a CSS engine. That is why CSS Color 4 adopted it, making it the first perceptual space available with no library at all, and why design-token and theme generators moved to it wholesale.
algorithms.citation: Ottosson, A perceptual color space for image processing, 2020; adopted in W3C CSS Color Module Level 4

algorithms.name: PCGRL — level generation as a reinforcement learning task
algorithms.authors: Ahmed Khalifa, Philip Bontrager, Sam Earle, Julian Togelius
algorithms.summary: Train an agent whose actions edit a level and whose reward is how much the edit improved it. Generation becomes a policy, not a search.
algorithms.eli5: Rather than searching for a good level each time one is wanted, train something to edit levels: it observes the current layout, changes one tile, and receives a small reward if that improved the level against the criteria you care about. Once trained it produces a level in a few dozen edits, and it never needed any example levels to learn from.
algorithms.description: The level is the environment state, tile edits are the actions, and the reward is the improvement in a quality measure — path length, reachability, region count — evaluated by the same kind of function a search-based generator would use as fitness. The paper defines three representations differing in how much control the agent has over where it edits: narrow, where the position is given and the agent only chooses content; turtle, where it also moves; and wide, where it chooses both position and content freely. Two things distinguish this from evolutionary search. It needs no training data, because the reward function supplies the signal, which sidesteps the small-dataset problem that limits most PCGML. And the expensive part happens once during training, so generation afterwards is a forward pass rather than a search — the difference between a generator you can call in a level-loading screen and one you cannot. The known weaknesses are limited output diversity and reward hacking, both of which are the fitness function's failings rather than the method's.
algorithms.citation: Khalifa, Bontrager, Earle & Togelius, PCGRL: procedural content generation via reinforcement learning, AIIDE 2020

algorithms.name: Practical real-time hex-tiling
algorithms.summary: A production-oriented refinement of histogram-preserving blending, addressing normal maps and cost for real-time use.
algorithms.eli5: Cover the surface with overlapping hexagons instead of squares, place a randomly rotated copy of the texture in each, and blend the overlaps using the contrast-preserving transform above. No visible repetition and no visible seams, from one texture and roughly twenty lines of shader.
algorithms.description: Heitz and Neyret's method assumes it is blending a scalar or colour signal, which breaks for normal and derivative maps where naive averaging produces wrong lighting rather than just wrong contrast. Mikkelsen's version handles those channels correctly, reduces the number of texture fetches needed per pixel, and adds practical controls for how hard the blend transitions between hex cells so artists can trade repetition against softness. It is the version that actually ships in engines, and the pairing is a good illustration of why the algorithm layer needs both entries: one paper established the method, a second made it usable.
algorithms.citation: Practical Real-Time Hex-Tiling, Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques 11(3)

algorithms.name: Latent diffusion
algorithms.authors: Robin Rombach, Andreas Blattmann, Dominik Lorenz, Patrick Esser, Björn Ommer
algorithms.summary: Run the diffusion process in a compressed latent space rather than on pixels. Two orders of magnitude cheaper, and where conditioning attaches.
algorithms.eli5: Denoising a full-resolution image a thousand times over is enormously expensive, and most of that effort goes on detail the eye barely registers. So first train a compressor that reduces images to a much smaller grid and back with little visible loss, run the entire denoising process on the small grid, and expand only at the end.
algorithms.description: Two stages. An autoencoder with a perceptual and adversarial objective compresses images to a latent grid — typically 8× smaller per side, so 64× fewer elements — retaining what matters visually while discarding imperceptible high-frequency detail. The diffusion model then operates entirely in that latent space, which cuts both training and sampling cost by roughly two orders of magnitude and is what made high-resolution generation runnable on consumer hardware. The second contribution is architectural: cross-attention layers inserted into the denoising U-Net accept an arbitrary conditioning sequence, so text, layouts, semantic maps and other images all attach through one general mechanism rather than needing bespoke models. This is the architecture behind Stable Diffusion and therefore behind most open image generation, and it is the practical answer to the `ml` concept card's complaint about control: the conditioning interface, not the diffusion, is what made these models directable.
algorithms.citation: Rombach, Blattmann, Lorenz, Esser & Ommer, High-resolution image synthesis with latent diffusion models, CVPR 2022

algorithms.name: 3D Gaussian splatting
algorithms.authors: Bernhard Kerbl, Georgios Kopanas, Thomas Leimkühler, George Drettakis
algorithms.summary: Represent a scene as millions of anisotropic 3D Gaussians and rasterise them. NeRF quality, real-time speed.
algorithms.eli5: Represent a scene as a few million soft, stretched, coloured blobs positioned in space. To render, project them onto the screen back to front and blend. Because that is only drawing blobs, it is fast — and because each blob's position, shape and colour can be adjusted, photographs can be used to tune all of them at once.
algorithms.description: Replace the neural network with an explicit cloud of 3D Gaussians, each with a position, anisotropic covariance, opacity and view-dependent colour. Rendering projects each Gaussian to screen space and alpha-blends them front to back — rasterisation, not raymarching, so there is no network evaluation per sample and it runs at well over thirty frames per second. Fitting is gradient descent against photographs, as with NeRF, but with an adaptive densification step that clones Gaussians in under-reconstructed regions and prunes transparent ones, so the representation grows where detail is needed. It effectively displaced NeRF for practical capture within a year, and it matters to this catalogue because it moves learned scene representation from an offline curiosity into something a real-time engine can actually display.
algorithms.citation: Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler & Drettakis, 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering, ACM TOG 42(4) (SIGGRAPH 2023)

algorithms.name: The hat — an aperiodic monotile
algorithms.authors: David Smith, Joseph Samuel Myers, Craig S. Kaplan, Chaim Goodman-Strauss
algorithms.summary: A single shape that tiles the plane only aperiodically. The 'einstein' problem, open for sixty years, solved.
algorithms.eli5: For fifty years it was unknown whether a single tile shape could cover the plane without the arrangement ever repeating. In 2023 an amateur found one — a thirteen-sided shape assembled from eight kites — and it works, provided its mirror image may also be used.
algorithms.description: The question left open by Wang and narrowed by Penrose was whether one shape alone could force aperiodicity — the 'einstein' problem, from ein Stein, one stone. The hat is a polykite: eight kites obtained by cutting a hexagon through its edge midpoints. It tiles the plane using both the shape and its mirror image, and no arrangement of it is ever periodic. The proof works by showing the tiling decomposes into a hierarchy of larger metatiles that repeats the structure at every scale, so no translation can map it to itself. A follow-up produced the 'spectre', which achieves the same without needing reflections. Practically it offers the strongest form of repeat-free coverage from a single asset, and it is recent enough that almost nothing has been built on it.
algorithms.citation: An aperiodic monotile, arXiv:2303.10798 (2023)

algorithms.name: The spectre — a chiral aperiodic monotile
algorithms.authors: David Smith, Joseph Samuel Myers, Craig Kaplan, Chaim Goodman-Strauss
algorithms.summary: A single tile that tiles the plane only aperiodically and needs no reflected copies. The hat, fixed.
algorithms.eli5: The hat resolved the question with a caveat: its mirror image is also required, which is arguably two shapes. Two months later the same team removed the caveat. Take the equilateral member of the hat's family, curve its edges so a mirrored copy physically cannot fit, and one shape tiles forever without repeating and without ever being turned over.
algorithms.description: The hat belongs to a continuous family of polygons parameterised by two edge lengths, and the equilateral member of that family — which the paper calls the Tile(1,1) — is weakly chiral: it admits aperiodic tilings using only unreflected copies, although reflected tilings also exist. Replacing its straight edges with matching curves gives the spectre family, which is strictly chiral: reflected copies simply cannot be placed, so every tiling is aperiodic and unreflected, built from a hierarchical substitution system. That closes the question the hat left open, since a monotile that requires its own mirror image is arguably not a single tile at all. For anything physical the distinction is decisive — a cut tile, a printed one-sided sheet, a set of moulded pavers cannot be flipped — and this is the entry the catalogue was missing while asserting on the concept card that the hat gave repeat-free coverage on its own.
algorithms.citation: Smith, Myers, Kaplan & Goodman-Strauss, A chiral aperiodic monotile, arXiv:2305.17743 (2023); Combinatorial Theory 4(2), 2024
